---
title: "Computer Graphics — Rotate Every Point With One Matrix"
description: "A compact linear-algebra lesson with mathematical definitions, real values and reasoning."
---

## Start with a question

A small arrow points east. How can a graphics program rotate it 90° counterclockwise without hand-moving every point?

## Understand the central idea

A rotation is a linear transformation represented by a matrix. One multiplication moves any input coordinate pair.

## Express it with mathematics

$$
R_{90}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-y\\x\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** R₉₀ is a rotation by 90 degrees counterclockwise; x,y are input coordinates; −y,x are the new coordinates. The matrix represents the transformation relative to standard axes.

**Substitute real numbers:** For point (3,2), the result is (−2,3). The original squared distance is 3²+2²=13; the new squared distance is (−2)²+3²=13, so rotation preserved length.

## Why this works

The two columns are the rotated basis vectors: (1,0) becomes (0,1), and (0,1) becomes (−1,0). Linearity then determines every other point's image.

## What can go wrong?

Rotations around a point other than the origin need translation as well; homogeneous coordinates are commonly used to represent such affine operations.

## Your turn

Rotate (0,−2) once, then again. Where do you end up?
